summary:
We developed Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, a free browser game where kids aged 7–12 command a small outpost on Mars or the Moon for 12 days. Each day, the Sun provides limited power cells. Players split them between life support, the greenhouse, the radiation shield, and science and radio. There's never enough for everything, so every choice has a cost.

The game addresses the challenge by turning real NASA and CSA data into hands-on decisions. Live NASA DONKI solar flare data appears on the home screen, and archived real flares trigger in-game storms. Radiation doses come from OSDR RadLab, Curiosity RAD and Chang'e-4 measurements, and daily reports link to real OSDR space biology studies. Mars brings dust storms and delayed messages from Earth, while the Moon brings a long, dark lunar night. Read-aloud briefings, a Jargon Decoder and a kid-friendly glossary make the science easy to follow.

This matters because future explorers learn best by doing. Kids learn why astronauts must plan for space weather, grow food early, and make careful engineering trade-offs, just like real mission teams.
details:
What it does: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free browser game where kids aged 7–12 run an outpost on Mars or the Moon for 12 days. Each day, the Sun provides a limited number of power cells. Players split them between life support, the greenhouse, the radiation shield, and science and radio. They can pick one of three ready-made plans or set each system with + and − buttons. Capcom Dr. Stella Vance gives a daily briefing that can be read aloud. Players can tap modules and crew in the outpost scene to learn what each does. After each day, a report explains what happened and why, linked to a real NASA study. If air or crew health hits zero, the mission stops right away with a clear lesson. Every run ends with a chart and a "What You Learned" summary.

Real data: live NASA DONKI solar flares appear on the home screen. Archived DONKI flares and solar particle events trigger in-game storms. Daily radiation doses come from OSDR RadLab, Curiosity RAD and Chang'e-4 LND measurements. Daily facts link to OSDR space biology studies. Mars Trek, Moon Trek and the CSA Food Production toolkit shaped the two sites and the greenhouse. Simplified numbers, such as storm chances and crop growth times, are clearly labelled.

Benefits and impact: kids learn real engineering trade-offs by doing, not reading. They see why astronauts plan for space weather, grow food early, store power for dark or dusty days, and decide things alone when messages from Earth are delayed. The goal is to spark curiosity about space careers and show kids that real NASA data is open to everyone.

Creativity: two worlds with different hazards: Martian dust storms and day-late messages, and the long lunar night on the Moon. The game changes every run. Failure is instant and teaches something. A Jargon Decoder gives pronunciation, read-aloud and a quiz for each space word.

What we considered: reading level and accessibility for young kids, using few scrolls and clicks, honest labelling of live, archived and simplified data.

Tools: React, TypeScript, Vite, the NASA Open APIs, the OSDR and RadLab APIs, and GitHub Pages. For the demo video: FFmpeg, Piper neural text-to-speech, and resvg. Super Intelligence (AI) tools helped write the code, script and edit the demo video, draw the cartoon characters, and generate the narration voices. All SI content is disclosed in watermarks and metadata.
